# Top 5 posts from r/MovieSuggestions day

## 1. Just rewatched Reign of Fire (2002)for the first time in a few years

**Score:** 92
**Body:** And boy does it hold up. Christian bale, A relatively unknown Gerard Butler, and of course, bald bearded matthew mcconaughey. Awesome special effects and some pretty great looking practical effects and story. Dragons look great for 2002 standards. Quick and easy fun ride. 

### Top 8 comments and their replies (up to depth 10)

1. "What a DUMP"
  - He’s so perfect in this. Also didn’t realize the helicopter pilot actress is Natalya from Goldeneye. 
  - " We can this easy, or we can do this real easy"
2. Those dragons and the one from the 80’s movie Dragonslayer are my all time favorites.
3. Its a great watch, especially with alot of the stars being quite young at the time, as you said, Bale, Butler, Mccnauhey. Also it was two actors/actresses from another of my favourite movies, Vertical Limit,  The SFX even to this day isnt terrible, and the scenery is fantastic
4. Still holds up insanely well. McConaughey goes full apocalypse mode
  - Dude with that Viking axe. Hard as fuck 
5. this movie has aged way better than it had any right to
6. My favourite, heroic death in movie history. 

Also one of my top popcorn (press play and switch off brain) movies too 🐉👍
7. Iirc theres an interview with Bale  saying that he prepared for the role by dieting, since it was post apocalyptic scenario and resources are scarce and then in comes McConaughey all jacked. 🤣

## 2. Movies that are so bad they're hilariously great?

**Score:** 58
**Body:** I need much, much more of this in my life! 

Not looking for any intentionally bad movies such as Sharknado or Birdemic, I'd specifically like movies that were trying to be good and serious, and just ended up so bad that they're funny. 

I have seen The Room (2003) plenty of times, but the other one I really love is Replicas (2018) starring Keanu Reeves and Thomas Middleditch from Silicon Valley. It's actually a decent concept of a film, but is so riddled with plot holes, bad CGI and terrible acting from Keanu Reeves. It takes maybe 20 minutes for it to start getting really funny and absurd, but it is absolutely goofy and 100% worth a watch. I've watched it twice this year and it still makes me laugh out loud now. 

Those two are my recommendations! Also a quick shoutout to Red Letter Media's Best of the Worst series on YouTube! 


RECOMMENDATION EDIT: Okay, I can't find the comment but thank you to whoever suggested Serenity starting Matthew McConaughey! It is like a really bad Christopher Nolan movie, PLEASE watch this if you haven't!

  - YOU CAN’T PISS ON HOSPITALITY!

**Score:** 44
**Body:** I’m okay with any type of horror I’m just not into movies with a focus on romance. 

Even some crime/mystery/thriller movies are okay but I’m mainly looking for horror. I’m mainly into 70s/80s movies but I’m okay with any era. I also like a lot of extreme horror. Even some dark cinema that’s not necessarily horror/thriller territory is okay with me. 

I’m just looking for some movies not set in a hot environment at ALL. Cold/snow/winter/autumn. Anything like that. Thank you:)

# Top 5 posts from r/TrueFilm day

## 1. Teenage Sex and Death at Camp Miasma - my take as a trans person

**Score:** 138
**Body:** I've seen a lot of takes saying this movie only works for white, queer AFAB viewers because it's "sapphic." I get where that's coming from, but stopping at "they're lesbians and this is about sapphic sexuality" misses the whole point, I fear. 

What got me was the depiction of sex and dysphoria. Every sexual moment in this film is coated in discomfort, from Kris explaining her poly relationship to the KFC dipping sauce scene to her hyperfixation on her own sexual awakening. Kris doesn't have language for sex, desire, or her own body. It takes meeting someone who actually gets it, Billie, before she can open up at all. She has to dissociate from her own body just to approach anything sexual, or even talk about it. 

I don't read Kris as a cis woman. I read her as a trans woman still deep in dysphoria about her body and her sex organs, and that's reinforced by her fantasy of being the bimbo "last girl" in a horror movie. She wants to be seen, felt, and heard as a woman... But her dysphoria and subsequent dissociation surrounding this is amplified by the whole style of the movie shifting in and out of reality. The lines get really blurred between what's real and what's not. 

Little Death is the scary trans monster transphobes swear is coming for their kids. And it's that monster, taking Kris over, guided by Billie (the first person who actually sees and understands her), that finally lets Kris come into herself, her sexuality, and her body's place in all of it.

Every time I read a take from a cis queer viewer, I feel like I'm in that Zoom meeting with Kris, watching her explain the movie's whole allegory while it sails right over everyone's head. Even the queer assistant, who thinks they get it and chimes in, only to have Kris go "actually, no, you don't."

### Top 8 comments and their replies (up to depth 10)

1. > I've seen a lot of takes saying this movie only works for white, queer AFAB viewers because it's "sapphic."

I generally hate takes like this. The vast majority of films in cinematic history star straight white men, are we supposed to believe that only straight white men ever got any value from them? 

I'm cis, I'm straight, and I enjoy Schoenbrun's films. Heaven forbid I be able to take anything of value from queer media, or any media that isn't centered on my specific sexuality?

None of which is to say that the queer perspective isn't relevant, it absolutely is. But as Roger Ebert once said, movies are "a machine that generates empathy." The whole point is to put ourselves in someone else's shoes, in someone else's circumstances, and indeed, in someone else's sexuality, should the film call for it. Oftentimes, the more personal the story is for the filmmakers, the better.

I don't know if OP is correct that Kris is a trans woman. It's plainly possible and common that a trans person who's lived a trans person's life will pick up on nuances that I can't with my own life experiences. But I do know you don't have to be a cis lesbian to get something from *Teenage Sex and Death at Camp Miasma* any more than you have to be white or straight to get something from, say, *Eternal Sunshine of the Spotless Mind,* even if being a specific flavor of queer will get you something out of a given film that you otherwise couldn't get. 

There will always be something for everyone else to empathize with. At least, assuming it's a good film.
2. Thoughtful take. 

This is probably a jarring shift in tone, but one of my favorite moments in the movie is when queer assistant keeps looking away from their web cam during the pitch (blatantly on off-camera iphone). Great scene for the webcam role, glad you enjoyed them too.
  - Yes!! I noticed that queer assistant just seemed generally bored before piping in with the half-ass "oh, it's a meta thing..." 

I thought it was funny commentary on like.. performative queer allies? Or moreso a funny callback to Kris' earlier monologue about Hollywood execs/studios including queer people in the room just to check that "we're woke" box. Queer Assistant understands that's why they're there... So they're just bored and getting through the day, sitting through who knows how many pitch meetings basically just like this one. 
    - Like Julio Torres’ “blue haired barista”
3. Great write-up. I'm reminded of Bride of Chucky and Tiffany explaining that an orgasm is called Le Petit Mort in French AKA little death.

That orgasm had been seeking the protagonist out forever and when she finally let go, they found each other.
4. I haven't seen people say that the movie isn't trans, but discounting the obvious trans elements certainly seems like a shallow viewing of the film. The slasher is a gender non-conforming person who's named after the French term for orgasms. Trans sexuality is pretty bluntly a part of the themes. 

Plus Kris and Owen from I Saw the TV Glow both have the character trait about being more interested in media than sex, it's pretty bluntly something Schoenbrun (a non-binary person) is working through in these characters.
  - What's this about slashers being named after orgasms?

Edit: thank you for the explanation! I was reading it as "the slasher" the trope not "the slasher named little death". Because a lot of historical slasher characters are kind of genderless too. I'm thinking Ghostface for sure, Michael Myers and Leatherface to a degree.
5. This was my takeaway too, i really love how you put it with this post. I really feel like the flashing of little death as a screaming child in Kris's mirror is hard to explain otherwise. 

Thanks for typing this up!
6. I think something incredibly telling is the sequence where we see an unmasked, monstrous Little Death as Kris looks in the mirror, as well as seeing that same horrific face projected over the top of the Little Death cardboard cutout. 

As a trans woman, it was a perfect portrayal of how transphobic caricatures negatively impact intimacy and self-image. I struggle personally with the imagery often used by Republican political cartoonists, where they draw trans women as these hideous creatures of gross hairy men in dresses, and that imagery can become incredibly harmful to any part of you that wants to feel desired and seen as a sexual being. 

There's also layers to it as well, as the movie is also about the notion of reclamation of problematic media within the queer community. Case in point, the Sleepaway Camp franchise is at once horrendously transphobic and also many weird trans horror fans' first exposure to ideas of gender identity. I know that it's a franchise that I think about a lot, but no matter how much I try to reclaim it, there's still the fact that it's based on some pretty fucked up underlying assumptions (I appreciate the camp miasma parody tagline: "they drowned him. They had to."). Even if you reclaim something as being important to you, it still can present an obstacle to seeing yourself fully and beautifully. Queer people often idolize the queer coded villains in media but at some point you have to unpack that and find a way to be the heroic protagonist in your narrative. 
7. As a cis woman who hasn't seen it yet (Friday!), I thought it was commonly acknowledged that this is what it's about. I mean look who directed it and her past work? Hello??? 

To be clear I'm not directing any negativity at you, I'm just surprised to learn via your post that people are being this dense. I don't know why I'm surprised at this point - maybe I thought the audience for this movie, which is pretty self-selecting, would be more tapped in.

## 2. The Proposition on Rewatch

**Score:** 61
**Body:** Rewatched John Hillcoat's Australian western *The Proposition* last night. Gotta say, it still remains one of my favorite westerns despite discovering it only a few years ago.

By far the best quality about it is Hillcoat's dismantling of the western genre. There's no romance, no beauty, or the slightest moment of humor in *The Proposition*. It's pure unremitting despair in a world so devoid of hope and full of violence it makes Clint Eastwood's *Unforgiven* seem cheery. Roger Ebert wrote in his [review](https://www.rogerebert.com/reviews/the-proposition-2006) how the film feels close to being an adaptation of Cormac McCarthy's *Blood Meridian* and boy, he was not wrong. Though a different tale, *The Proposition* is not only unflinching in its violence, but it never feels cinematic nor sensationalized compared to other westerns. Furthermore, it also has the same kind of bleak setting full of characters that are almost morally reprehensible in one way or another. The fact John Hillcoat is said to be working on the film adaptation of *Blood Meridian* really shows how *The Proposition* is very similar tonally and thematically.

The decision to set it  in 1880s Australia under British colonialism too is genuinely original. The unique setting perfectly fits with the film's dark narrative and characters, sometimes even making it feel like a loose adaptation of Joseph Conrad's *Heart of Darkness* in depicting colonization in a land that is hostile to non-natives. The way Captain Stanley wants to bring order to the land but fails to due to its hostile nature in many scenes really emphasizes this aspect. 

Of course, Nick Cave's screenplay deserves much credit as this is such a smartly written western. The setup is simple, yet there are so many moments where much is said without dialogue between characters and their relationships. And when the characters do speak, it's incredibly engaging dialogue that brings a unique life to each character, especially the monologue from John Hurt that arguably is the best scene in the film. 

All of this too is backed up by many great performances from Guy Pearce, Ray Winstone, John Hurt, and Danny Huston who, on rewatch, I think gives the best performance by far. The way he plays Arthur Burns as a cold-blooded, emotionless bandit who philosophies about life is genuinely unnerving, with even Ebert stating his character to feel like a takeoff of the Judge character in *Blood Meridian*. 

To me, *The Proposition* is easily the most underrated western of the 2000s and possibly of all time. It borrows from many anti-western inspirations, yet John Hillcoat and Nick Cave take it in a vastly different direction. And the score by Nick Cave and Warren Ellis? Absolutely haunting.

  
Source: Ebert, Roger. "Blood on the saddle." *Roger Ebert,* 18 May 2006, https://www.rogerebert.com/reviews/the-proposition-2006.

### Top 3 comments and their replies (up to depth 10)

1. I think it’s a classic and it’s been a favourite of my for quite some time. The natural landscape plays such a ruthless character that it emphasises the incredible hubris required of men like Captain Stanley to believe that they can stand up to it. Glad you mentioned the haunting score too, that eerie violin stays with you and I can think of many other films of this level where the same person is responsible for both story and music.
2. Love this film and John Hillcoat he is a legend. I would highly reccommend another film of his, Ghosts of the Civil Dead. I watched it maybe a year back and it made me feel like I was being haunted for days, superb and unique film.
3. Interesting. I'll have to give it a second look. I was unaffected by *The Proposition*. But the allusions to McCarthy's work and *Blood Meridian* in particular might be why. I'm in the minority, I suppose, but I can't stand *Blood Meridian* or most of McCarthy's work (I suppose). *No Country for Old Men* is one of the dumbest films (a separate conversation).

But the common denominator I think is McCarthy's too dire view of humanity. He goes beyond nihilism and just plainly states that the *Bad guys always win* (and somehow he had a successful career as a writer...).

It's not that I think Westerns shouldn't go against the grain or be "anti" or that a gritty realism isn't wanted or even necessary. My third favorite film and IMO the best Western ever probably falls within your traditional western genre, but I think it's an anti-western, Once Upon a Time in the West.

Also, depending on the type of film/genre, I'm of the preference that dead bodies should have their eyes open in most cases. When westerns avoid that they miss out on a level of realism that I think would greatly help. Anyone who's seen old timey photos of dead bandits on display in their coffins knows what I'm talking about. I even included that scene in my western.

I just think that absolute evil and unremitting despair are not realistic either. The fact is that if the "Wild West," in any country, had been that bad, we'd all be dead. Mad Max would have happened by the '50s. I think this is why The Seven Samurai strikes such a perfect balance (oddly enough, not so much The Magnificent Seven(s)).
  - Fair argument. I will admit *The Proposition* is a bleak film that doesn’t go easy. I can understand your dislike of McCarthy’s writing as his works often are harsh to the point that it can feel like overkill. The only exception to that is possibly his most loved novel, *The Road*, but even that is incredibly grim with very faint glimmers of light.

Glad to see you’re also a fan of *Once Upon a Time in the West*. For me, that’s still admittedly my favorite western overall. Sergio Leone really took what he learned from the Dollars trilogy and honed it to perfection in OUATITW along with Ennio Morricone.
    - Oh! Hillcoat also directed *The Road*.
  - I don’t think it’s going to happen, but imagine if Blood Meridian had gone through production with Hillcoat as director.

That’s interesting, because I never had an issue with McCarthy’s nihilism.  I just hated his prose.  Which is why I particularly liked No Country for Old Men.  Because it largely avoided his Anne Poulx-style gobbledygook by being a screen treatment 
    - Calling McCarthy gobbledygook is certainly a claim. Blood Meridian is easily up there with the greatest novels of all time.
      - I know many folks think that. 

## 3. Does this bit of trivia defy the whole point of natural born killers?

**Score:** 23
**Body:** &#x200B;

In the mess hall in the prison, a bald white man is staring at a black man, prompting the black man to try to attack him, before being intercepted by Warden McClusky (Tommy Lee Jones). The bald man was a real prisoner, who had been convicted of murdering his wife and children by beating them to death with a lead pipe. Oliver Stone gave him a featured role, because he said the man's stoicism terrified him.

https://www.imdb.com/title/tt0110632/trivia?item=tr0774748

## 5. Lovers of the Arctic Circle: when a film’s structure starts behaving like its characters’ idea of fate

**Score:** 7
**Body:** One of the things that stayed with me from *Lovers of the Arctic Circle* is its obsession with circularity.

Even the names Ana and Otto are palindromes. They can be read in both directions, returning to where they began. The film seems to construct their relationship in much the same way: departures become returns, coincidences accumulate, perspectives repeat events differently, and the story keeps suggesting that Ana and Otto are moving around some invisible center.

What interests me is whether Medem wants us to believe in that idea of fate, or whether he is showing us how people create patterns when they desperately need their lives to have one.

Coincidence in the film rarely feels neutral. Ana and Otto interpret events, encounters and repetitions as though they belong to a larger design. And because the film itself is organized around circles, mirrored perspectives and recurrence, the cinematic form seems to validate their belief.  
But there’s another possibility.

Maybe the film isn’t demonstrating that their lives are governed by fate. Maybe we’re experiencing reality through two people who have become so invested in their shared story that everything begins to look like evidence that the story must continue.

If the coincidences are objectively meaningful, *Lovers of the Arctic Circle* is a romantic tragedy about two people repeatedly brought together by fate.  
If they aren’t, it becomes something stranger: a film about the human tendency to turn coincidence into narrative and narrative into destiny.

Do you think Medem ultimately asks us to believe in Ana and Otto’s fate, or does the film deliberately leave open the possibility that the “circle” exists mainly because they, and perhaps we as viewers, need to see one?
